description: small team aiming to build something innovative
summary:
Moon Base Mission is a free browser game that trains young astronauts to keep a Moon base alive for 12 days. Each day, players share a few power cells between life support, a radiation shield and science. There is never enough for everything, so every choice is a real trade-off, just like the ones mission planners face.

Three solar storms hit during each mission. Every storm is based on a real solar flare from NASA's DONKI space weather database, and players can see each flare on a chart and open its NASA record. When the long lunar night arrives, solar power drops and players must rely on the energy they saved.

A friendly guide named Pip makes the game beginner friendly: a short briefing, a first-day tour, and daily advice that warns players before things go wrong. In the Mission Lab, players test strategies with the scientific method: they make a hypothesis and run a fair test of 2,000 simulated missions. The game runs on any phone or computer with no install, so any classroom can use it.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Moon Base Mission is a turn-based strategy game. The player commands a Moon base with four astronauts for 12 days. Each day the solar panels give a few power cells, and the player places them on:

- Life support (makes air; the crew breathes 20 air a day)

- Radiation shield (protects the crew from solar storms)

- Science lab (earns points, but keeps nothing safe)

Cells that aren't used are saved in a battery. After 6 to 8 days the lunar night begins and solar power drops, so players have to plan ahead. The mission ends early if air or crew health reaches zero.

HOW IT USES NASA DATA

When the game starts, it loads the last 30 days of solar flares from NASA's DONKI database through api.nasa.gov. Three of those flares become the mission's storms: C-class flares make small storms, M-class medium and X-class big. Players get a space weather alert one day before each storm. A chart shows every flare by strength, and each storm links to its NASA record. If the API can't be reached, the game uses real flares from 2024 and clearly labels them as archived.

BEGINNER FRIENDLY

Pip, an astronaut guide, gives a 7-step briefing with a practice row, a first-day tour that highlights each part of the screen, and daily advice that checks the player's plan (for example: "the air runs out in about 3 days"). The whole game fits on one laptop screen, and phones get a status bar that stays at the top.

THE SCIENTIFIC METHOD

In the Mission Lab, players pick a question and a hypothesis, then the game runs a fair test: every strategy faces exactly the same 500 missions, and only the plan changes. The results are surprising. Doing the same thing every day survives only about 10% of missions, while watching the space weather survives almost every time. This shows why scientists test ideas instead of guessing.

STORYTELLING AND IMPACT

An international crew from India, Canada, Japan and Brazil writes a log after each day that reacts to the player's choices. The debrief connects the lessons to Earth: solar power and batteries for off-grid communities, how space weather can disturb satellites, GPS and power grids, and how to share limited resources.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGY

One HTML file using HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with no libraries. All graphics (Pip, the crew, the Moon scene, the charts) are SVG drawn in code, and all sounds are generated live with the Web Audio API. Hosted free on GitHub Pages. We tested it with 20,000 simulated games and random-click browser tests, and confirmed that every mission can be won.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED

Young players need to understand the rules without reading a manual, so we kept only three systems and added a guide. Accuracy matters, so the game is clear about what is simplified: the numbers are game balance, not engineering values. It needs to work in schools with weak internet, so it is a single small file that also works offline.

NEXT STEPS

Tamil and Hindi versions for local schools, a Mars mode with communication delay, and astronaut health data from NASA's Open Science Data Repository.
